results.title: Don't Throw Away Your Pits! Grow Peach, Plum, Cherry, Apricot & Almond Trees in Just 3 Steps
results.description:
What if the peach, plum, cherry, apricot, or almond pit you were about to throw away could become a tree?

In this video, we're showing you how to grow peach, plum, cherry, apricot, and almond trees from pits in 3 simple steps. These fruits belong to the Prunus group and produce stone fruits, meaning the seed is protected inside a hard pit.

You'll learn the complete process, from cleaning and preparing the pit to cold stratification, planting, and caring for the young seedling.

🌱 In this video you'll learn:
How to properly clean and prepare fruit pits
Why starting with several pits can improve your chances of success
What cold stratification means and why it matters
How long peach, apricot, plum, cherry, and almond pits may need cold treatment
How to plant a sprouted pit correctly
How deep to plant the pit
Why keeping the soil moist—but not soggy—is important
Why newly sprouted seedlings should receive gentle light initially
Why fruit grown from seed may not be identical to the fruit you originally ate
Important safety considerations when handling raw fruit pits
Climate and winter considerations for growing these trees

The cold-stratification stage is especially important in the method presented here. The script recommends placing cleaned pits in a slightly damp paper towel inside a bag and refrigerating them for several weeks, with the timing varying by fruit.

And there's one more thing every beginner should understand: growing a tree from a pit doesn't guarantee that the eventual fruit will be an exact copy of the original fruit. Seed-grown trees can differ genetically from their parent fruit, making the process more of a long-term gardening experiment.

From something that almost went into the trash to a tree growing in your backyard, this is one of the most rewarding ways to explore what your fruit seeds can become.

Subscribe to @ROOTANDREMEDIES8 for more practical, beginner-friendly gardening ideas, growing experiments, seasonal plant care, and ways to get more from the food you already have.


 DISCLAIMER

Growing fruit trees from pits can take considerable time, and germination, growth, hardiness, flowering, and fruiting can vary by species, variety, climate, and growing conditions. A seed-grown tree may also produce fruit that differs from the original fruit because it is not necessarily genetically identical to its parent tree.

The timing and hardiness information in this video is general guidance. The script notes that these fruits commonly grow across a range of USDA zones, with specific varieties and local conditions affecting their performance.

Safety note: Peach, plum, cherry, apricot, and some almond pits/kernels contain naturally occurring cyanogenic compounds. Do not treat raw pits or kernels as food, and keep them away from children and pets while handling them.

results.description:
Your Peach Pit Grows a Real Tree — But Your Cherry Pit Won't. Here's Why.

Every peach, plum, cherry, apricot and almond pit you throw away is a living tree — but nobody tells you the whole truth about what grows out of it. I'm Mia, and in this video I'm walking you through the exact 3-step method I use to turn kitchen scraps into real fruit trees, completely free.

You'll learn why almost every pit-growing attempt fails (it's not your soil and it's not your skill), the cold-winter trick called stratification that switches the seed on, and the timing each fruit needs. I'm also answering the question everyone asks in the comments: "aren't fruit trees all grafted?" The honest answer surprises most people — peaches, apricots and nectarines pollinate themselves and grow remarkably close to the parent fruit, while cherries and apples are a genuine lottery. That's exactly why nurseries graft those, and it's exactly why they plant peach pits by the thousand.

And there's one warning I include that almost no guide mentions: the almond-shaped seed inside the pit is not a snack. Stick around to the end for that one — it matters, especially if you have kids or pets.

results.description:
Don’t throw away that peach pit. It may look like kitchen waste, but with the right cold treatment, it can become the beginning of a real fruit tree.

In this Elder Gardens episode, we walk through the old-fashioned way to grow stone fruit trees from pits and seeds, including peaches, plums, cherries, apricots, nectarines, and almonds. The secret most gardeners miss is simple: these seeds need a “winter” before they wake up. Gardeners call it cold stratification, but all it really means is giving the seed the cold, damp season it was built to wait for.

You’ll learn why most peach pits never sprout on a windowsill, how long each type of stone fruit seed needs in the refrigerator, which fruits are more likely to grow close to the parent tree, and which ones are true wildcards. We’ll also cover how to clean the pit, test it in water, crack peach and apricot shells safely, use sand and perlite for stratification, watch for the first white root tip, and move your seedling into a pot without drowning it.

This video also explains the honest timeline: why a seed-grown peach may fruit sooner than cherries or plums, why nursery trees are often grafted, and how your free seedling can one day become strong rootstock for a grafted fruit tree.

Important safety note: stone fruit kernels may look like almonds, but they are not food. Handle them for planting only, and do not eat raw peach, apricot, cherry, plum, or almond-like kernels.
